To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(i) MAML is only effective if the tasks have a significant discrepancy in their hardness, and (ii ) the optimal solutions of easy tasks should be far from the optimal solutions of hard tasks, with the centers of the easy task optimal solutions far from the center.
MAML is more likely to outperform NAL when the optimal solution to a task is far from the center, and that MAML is likely to outperform when there are tasks of different difficulty.

MAML should be applied to a mixture of easy (converge quickly) and hard (converge slowly) tasks where there is a significant gap between the optimal solutions of easy and hard task and the optimal solution of easy task is close to the optimal solutions of hard tasks.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
MAML is a powerful tool for learning fast-adaptive solutions to a set of tasks when the tasks are heterogeneous and the optimal solutions are closely packed in the parameter space.
MAML is more effective in scenarios where there are significant differences among the tasks, but the difference is not too large.
